notes.title: Start here: MarketForge and its learning folder
notes.body:
This pack uses **MarketForge**, a Next.js marketplace in `marketplace/`: many sellers run stores, and buyers shop across all of them with one cart. Data lives in SQLite. The learning material is in `marketplace/_learning/`.

Read in this order:

- **_learning/00-ARCHITECTURE.md**: what the app does, the tech stack, and the main flows.
- **_learning/03-LEARNING-PATH.md**: chapters, each with a goal, files to read in order, a checkpoint and practice.
- **_learning/05-PATTERNS.md**: the patterns the code uses and the anti-patterns to avoid.
- **_learning/02-ARRAY-CHEATSHEET.md**: `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `find`, `some`, `sort` and friends, with a decision tree.
- **_learning/guides/**: one guide per source file.

The quizzes are about the business code in `marketplace/src/lib/`: `cart.js`, `orders.js`, `auth.js` and `security.js`. Each quiz gives a concrete situation. Work it out by running the numbers through the exact lines, as if you were the computer.

excerpts.quote: MarketForge is an online marketplace where many independent sellers can run stores and sell products, and buyers can shop across all those stores in one place.
This plan is ordered to maximize JavaScript fundamentals first, then full-stack application fluency.

readMore.why: The patterns and anti-patterns used across the code.

notes.title: Concept: thin API routes and domain modules
notes.body:
05-PATTERNS.md names the first pattern **Thin API Handler + Domain Service**: the API route does the HTTP plumbing, and a domain module in `src/lib/` does the business logic. For example `src/app/api/checkout/route.js` reads the request and calls `checkout` in `src/lib/orders.js`.

This is why every quiz in this pack points at a file in `src/lib/`. The rules live there:

- **cart.js**: finding the right cart, adding items, building the cart summary.
- **orders.js**: discounts, tax, splitting a checkout, inventory updates.
- **auth.js**: reading the session and checking roles.
- **security.js**: password hashing and money helpers.

Some functions run inside `runInTransaction` from `db.js`: a helper that starts a database transaction, runs your callback, and either commits or rolls back. When a quiz describes an error in the middle of a multi-step write, check whether the code is inside that helper.

excerpts.quote: - Plain English: API route does HTTP plumbing; domain module does business logic. - Where: `src/app/api/cart/route.js` + `src/lib/cart.js`, `src/app/api/checkout/route.js` + `src/lib/orders.js`. - Why useful: keeps route files readable and business rules reusable.

notes.title: Concept: money in whole cents and filter-map-reduce pipelines
notes.body:
Two habits run through the business code.

**Money is stored in integer cents.** A price of $19.99 is stored as 1999. Decimal money in JavaScript floats is risky, because values like 0.1 cannot be stored exactly, so totals drift. With whole cents, adding is exact. The cost: whenever you divide money (a percentage, a share), you must decide how to turn a fraction of a cent back into a whole number, and that choice changes totals. Watch for `Math.floor`, `Math.round` and `Math.min` around every money calculation.

**Data flows through small pipelines.** 05-PATTERNS.md calls it the data pipeline pattern: `filter` keeps the rows you want, `map` reshapes each one, and `reduce` folds a list into one value (a total, or an object grouping items by key). Reading a `reduce` carefully, especially its starting value and what it adds each step, is the key skill for most quizzes here. The array cheat sheet has a decision tree for choosing the method.

excerpts.quote: ## 3) Data Pipeline Pattern (`filter -> map -> reduce`) - Plain English: transform data in small composable stages.
**What it does**: Accumulates array items into one value.
export function toCents(value) { const numeric = Number(value); if (!Number.isFinite(numeric)) { return 0; } return Math.round(numeric * 100); }

notes.title: Why adding 3 to a line of 5 quietly gives 6
notes.body:
`addCartItem` first works out `requestedQuantity` (here 3) and checks `variant.inventory < requestedQuantity`: is 6 less than 3? No, so it does not throw. Note that this check looks only at the 3 being added, not at the 5 already in the cart. Then it finds the existing line for this variant and sets `nextQuantity = Math.min(existing.quantity + requestedQuantity, variant.inventory)` = `Math.min(8, 6)` = 6. The line is updated to 6, with no error or message.

Why the others are wrong:
- The throw compares only the requested 3 with the stock, so it does not fire.
- The quantity is clamped by `Math.min` to 6, not stored as 8.
- An existing line for the same variant is updated; a new line is inserted only when none exists.

excerpts.quote: const requestedQuantity = Math.max(1, Math.min(99, Number(quantity))); if (variant.inventory < requestedQuantity) { throw new Error("Not enough inventory for this variant"); }

if (existing) { const nextQuantity = Math.min(existing.quantity + requestedQuantity, variant.inventory); db.prepare("UPDATE cart_items SET quantity = ?, added_at = ? WHERE id = ?").run(nextQuantity, addedAt, existing.id);

notes.title: Why one seller's missing stock cancels the whole checkout
notes.body:
The inventory update is written so it can never oversell: `UPDATE ... SET inventory = inventory - ? WHERE id = ? AND inventory >= ?`. With 1 unit left and 2 wanted, the WHERE clause matches no row, so `changes === 0` and the code throws "Inventory changed for ...". The whole `checkout` runs inside `runInTransaction`, which starts with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE TRANSACTION`. When the callback throws, it runs `ROLLBACK`, and that undoes *everything* done in the transaction, including the first seller's order insert. So nothing is saved.

Why the others are wrong:
- The first order is inside the same transaction, so the rollback removes it too.
- The guarded UPDATE cannot take inventory below the quantity; it changes nothing and throws.
- The quantity is never reduced to what is left; the code throws instead.

excerpts.quote: const updateInventory = db .prepare( "UPDATE product_variants SET inventory = inventory - ? WHERE id = ? AND inventory >= ?" ) .run(item.quantity, item.variantId, item.quantity); if (updateInventory.changes === 0) { throw new Error(`Inventory changed for ${item.productTitle}. Please review your cart.`); }

export function runInTransaction(callback) { const db = getDb(); db.exec("BEGIN IMMEDIATE TRANSACTION"); try { const result = callback(db); db.exec("COMMIT"); return result; } catch (error) { db.exec("ROLLBACK"); throw error; }

notes.title: Why no session gives 401 but a buyer gets 403
notes.body:
`requireUser` asks two different questions in order. First: is anyone logged in? If `getCurrentUser()` returns no user, it throws "Unauthorized" with status **401**. Second: is this user allowed? If `allowedRoles` is not empty and does not include `user.role`, it throws "Forbidden" with status **403**. The visitor with no cookie fails the first question: 401. The logged-in BUYER passes the first and fails the second, since ADMIN is the only allowed role: 403. 401 means "I don't know who you are"; 403 means "I know who you are, and you may not do this".

Why the others are wrong:
- The buyer *is* authenticated, so 401 is wrong for them.
- No code returns 404 here.
- The visitor without a session never reaches the role check; they get 401.

excerpts.quote: if (!user) { const error = new Error("Unauthorized"); error.status = 401; throw error; } if (allowedRoles.length > 0 && !allowedRoles.includes(user.role)) { const error = new Error("Forbidden"); error.status = 403; throw error; }

notes.title: What happens to a saved-for-later item in totals and checkout
notes.body:
`buildCartSummary` starts by splitting the items: `activeItems = items.filter((item) => !item.savedForLater)` and `savedItems = items.filter((item) => item.savedForLater)`. Every total after that (seller groups, `subtotalCents`, `itemCount`) is computed from `activeItems` only. The saved item is returned separately as `savedForLater`, so it can be shown but is not counted. Checkout does the same: its first step is `getCartItemsRaw(cart.id).filter((item) => !item.savedForLater)`. So only the active item counts in the subtotal and is bought.

Why the others are wrong:
- The subtotal is summed from active items only.
- The saved item is the one left out, not the one kept; the order items were added in does not matter.
- Both totals and checkout filter saved items out.

excerpts.quote: const activeItems = items.filter((item) => !item.savedForLater); const savedItems = items.filter((item) => item.savedForLater);
const subtotalCents = activeItems.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.priceCents * item.quantity, 0);
const items = getCartItemsRaw(cart.id).filter((item) => !item.savedForLater);

notes.title: What getCurrentUser does with an expired session
notes.body:
The cookie only carries a token. `getCurrentUser` looks the token up in the `sessions` table, joined with the user, including `s.expires_at`. Then it checks: `if (new Date(row.expires_at).getTime() < Date.now())`. For an expired session that is true, so it deletes that session row (`DELETE FROM sessions WHERE token = ?`) and returns `null`. To the rest of the app the request is simply logged out. The expiry is decided by the server's database, not by whether the browser still has the cookie.

Why the others are wrong:
- Nothing extends the session; it is deleted.
- `getCurrentUser` returns null; throwing 401 is `requireUser`'s job.
- Having the cookie is not enough; the server checks the stored expiry.

excerpts.quote: if (new Date(row.expires_at).getTime() < Date.now()) { db.prepare("DELETE FROM sessions WHERE token = ?").run(token); return null; }
const row = db .prepare( `SELECT u.id, u.email, u.role, u.name, s.expires_at FROM sessions s JOIN users u ON u.id = s.user_id WHERE s.token = ?` ) .get(token);

notes.title: Why splitting a 1000-cent discount records only 999
notes.body:
Each seller gets a share of the discount in proportion to their part of the subtotal: `Math.floor((sellerSubtotal / subtotalCents) * discountCents)`.

- Seller A: 3333 / 10000 × 1000 = 333.3, floored to **333**.
- Seller B: 6667 / 10000 × 1000 = 666.7, floored to **666**.

333 + 666 = 999. Each `Math.floor` throws away a fraction of a cent, and nothing adds the lost cent back to anyone. This is a classic money-splitting bug: when you split an amount, the parts must be made to add up to the whole, for example by giving the remainder to one of them.

Why the others are wrong:
- The code floors; it does not round to nearest (which would give 333 + 667).
- There is no step that gives the leftover cent to a seller.
- Nothing rounds up.

excerpts.quote: const sellerSubtotal = sellerItems.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.priceCents * item.quantity, 0); const proportionalDiscount = subtotalCents > 0 ? Math.floor((sellerSubtotal / subtotalCents) * discountCents) : 0;

notes.title: How security.js stores and checks passwords
notes.body:
`hashPassword` makes a random 16-byte **salt** (`randomBytes(16)`), derives a 64-byte key with `scryptSync(password, salt, 64)`, and stores both as `salt:hash` in hex. A salt makes each stored hash unique, even for equal passwords. scrypt is deliberately slow and memory-hungry, which makes guessing expensive. `verifyPassword` splits the stored value, re-derives the hash from the typed password with the *same* salt, and compares with `timingSafeEqual`, which takes the same time however many bytes match. It checks the lengths first because `timingSafeEqual` requires equal-length inputs.

Why the others are wrong:
- It uses scrypt with a per-password salt, not SHA-256 with a pepper, and not `===`.
- The hash is salted; the salt is stored before the colon.
- No bcrypt is used.

excerpts.quote: const salt = randomBytes(16).toString("hex"); const hash = scryptSync(password, salt, 64).toString("hex"); return `${salt}:${hash}`;

const [salt, storedHash] = storedValue.split(":"); const computedHash = scryptSync(password, salt, 64).toString("hex"); const storedBuffer = Buffer.from(storedHash, "hex"); const computedBuffer = Buffer.from(computedHash, "hex"); if (storedBuffer.length !== computedBuffer.length) { return false; } return timingSafeEqual(storedBuffer, computedBuffer);

notes.title: Why checkout inserts one order per seller
notes.body:
`checkout` first groups the active items with `reduce`: `acc[item.sellerId] = acc[item.sellerId] ?? []` and pushes each item into its seller's list. Five items from three sellers become an object with three keys. Then `Object.entries(groupedBySeller).forEach(...)` runs once per seller, and each run inserts one order with that seller's items, its own discount share, tax and shipping. Three sellers, three orders; `orderIds` collects them. This matches the architecture guide: the app splits a checkout into separate seller orders.

Why the others are wrong:
- Orders are per seller, not per item.
- One order for everything would ignore the grouping.
- There is no parent order row; only one order per seller is inserted.

notes.title: Why a 5000-cent fixed code gives only 3000 off a 3000-cent cart
notes.body:
After the code is found and its checks pass (active, dates, minimum order, usage limit), the amount is computed: for PERCENT codes `Math.floor(subtotalCents * (row.amount / 100))`; otherwise, for fixed codes, `Math.min(row.amount, subtotalCents)`. `Math.min(5000, 3000)` is 3000. So a fixed discount can never be larger than the cart: at most the order becomes free.

Why the others are wrong:
- The total never goes negative; there is no refund logic.
- There is no half-the-subtotal cap.
- The code is not rejected for being larger than the subtotal; only a too-small order (`min_order_cents`) or other checks reject it.

excerpts.quote: const discountCents = row.type === "PERCENT" ? Math.floor(subtotalCents * (row.amount / 100)) : Math.min(row.amount, subtotalCents);
if (subtotalCents < row.min_order_cents) { throw new Error("Order does not meet discount minimum"); }

notes.title: How tax is worked out for a region not in the table
notes.body:
`REGION_TAX_RATE` lists CA, NY, TX and WA, plus `default: 0.06`. The checkout picks `REGION_TAX_RATE[payload.address.region] ?? REGION_TAX_RATE.default`. OR is not a key, so the lookup gives `undefined`, and `??` falls back to 0.06. Tax is then `Math.floor((sellerSubtotal - proportionalDiscount) * taxRate)`: tax is charged on the amount *after* the discount. That is (5000 − 500) × 0.06 = 4500 × 0.06 = 270, and the floor keeps 270.

Why the others are wrong:
- There is no "highest rate" fallback; the fallback is the default 6%.
- Tax is on the discounted amount, not the full 5000.
- Missing regions are not untaxed; they use the default rate.

excerpts.quote: const REGION_TAX_RATE = { CA: 0.0875, NY: 0.088, TX: 0.0825, WA: 0.065, default: 0.06 };
const taxRate = REGION_TAX_RATE[payload.address.region] ?? REGION_TAX_RATE.default;
const taxCents = Math.floor((sellerSubtotal - proportionalDiscount) * taxRate);

notes.title: Which cart wins when an anonymous shopper logs in
notes.body:
`resolveCart` looks for a cart in a fixed order. If there is a `userId`, it first looks for the user's cart. Only `if (!cart && sessionId)` does it look for the anonymous session cart. This account already has a cart, so the session lookup never happens and the user's cart is returned. The anonymous cart's items stay in that other cart; nothing merges them. The branch that sets `user_id` on a session cart only runs when the found cart has no user yet, which here is not the case.

Why the others are wrong:
- The anonymous cart is not returned, and nothing deletes the account's cart.
- No code combines two carts.
- Adopting the session cart (setting `user_id`) only happens when the user has no cart of their own.

excerpts.quote: if (userId) { cart = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM carts WHERE user_id = ?").get(userId); } if (!cart && sessionId) { cart = db.prepare("SELECT * FROM carts WHERE session_id = ?").get(sessionId); }
} else if (userId && !cart.user_id) { db.prepare("UPDATE carts SET user_id = ?, updated_at = ? WHERE id = ?").run(userId, nowIso(), cart.id); cart.user_id = userId; }
